concepts.name: Buddha Purnima (Vesak): Significance and Observance
key_dimensions: Triple significance: birth, enlightenment, and Mahaparinirvana of Buddha — all on the same full moon day of Vaisakha
Distinction between Theravada (Vesak) and Mahayana traditions in celebrating this festival
UN recognition of Vesak Day and India's diplomatic use of the festival for Buddhist heritage promotion
Common UPSC trap: conflating Buddha Purnima with Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din (different event, different date)

concepts.name: Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din: Historical and Constitutional Dimensions
key_dimensions: Marks the First Sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) at Sarnath — Ashada Purnima — distinct from Buddha Purnima
Adopted by B.R. Ambedkar as the date of his mass conversion to Buddhism in 1956 (Nagpur Deeksha Bhoomi)
Overlap with Guru Purnima — both fall on Ashadha Purnima, creating a recurring UPSC trap
Central government's official celebration and its role in Ambedkarite Buddhist movement

concepts.name: Asalha Puja (Dharma Day): Theravada Buddhist Observance
key_dimensions: Commemorates the first teaching of the Buddha and the establishment of the Sangha
Precedes the Vassa (Rains Retreat / Buddhist Lent) — a critical sequential relationship
Predominantly observed in Southeast Asian Theravada countries — relevance to India's Act East Policy
Distinction from Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din despite similar thematic content

concepts.name: Vassa (Rains Retreat / Varshavas): Monastic Discipline and Social Dimension
key_dimensions: Three-month retreat (Ashadha to Kartika) observed by Theravada monks — rooted in Vinaya Pitaka rules
Parallel with Jain Paryushana Parva — both are monsoon-season austerity periods, a common comparison question
Kathina ceremony at the end of Vassa — laity offering robes to monks, reinforcing lay-monk interdependence
Indian historical context: Ashoka's edicts reference non-killing of animals, possibly linked to retreat ethics

concepts.name: Losar: Tibetan Buddhist New Year Festival
key_dimensions: Celebrated by Tibetan, Ladakhi, and Sikkimese Buddhist communities — federalism/cultural diversity angle
Distinct from the Chinese New Year despite calendar overlap — UPSC trap on Sino-Tibetan cultural distinctions
Ritual components: Torma offerings, Cham dance (masked dance drama) — tangible intangible heritage overlap
Relevance to India's soft power in Himalayan border regions and Tibetan diaspora policy

concepts.name: Hemis Festival (Ladakh): Tantric Buddhism and Intangible Heritage
key_dimensions: Celebrates the birth of Guru Padmasambhava (Vajrayana tradition) — not mainstream Theravada/Mahayana
Cham dance as UNESCO-recognized intangible cultural heritage — masks, music, ritual drama
Held at Hemis Monastery, the largest in Ladakh — Drukpa Kagyu sect affiliation
UPSC angle: distinction between Guru Padmasambhava and Gautama Buddha — different figures, common confusion

concepts.name: Saga Dawa: Mahayana and Tibetan Buddhist Triple Holy Month
key_dimensions: Fourth lunar month considered most sacred — magnified karmic effects of actions (meritorious and non-meritorious)
Observed by Sikkim, Darjeeling, and Tibetan communities — India's northeastern Buddhist belt
Saga Dawa Düchen on the 15th day marks Buddha's enlightenment and parinirvana in Tibetan calendar — differs from Theravada Vesak dating
Trap: multiple Buddhist traditions celebrate 'enlightenment' on different dates — Theravada vs. Tibetan calendrical difference

concepts.name: Paryushana Parva: Core Jain Festival of Austerity and Ethics
key_dimensions: Most important Jain festival — 8 days for Shvetambara, 10 days (Das Lakshana) for Digambara
Culminates in Samvatsari (Shvetambara) / Uttam Kshama (Digambara) — the day of seeking universal forgiveness
Core ethical values emphasized: Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacharya, Aparigraha — direct link to Jain philosophy questions
UPSC trap: Shvetambara celebrates Samvatsari on 8th day; Digambara celebrates Das Lakshana Parva for 10 days — sectarian difference

concepts.name: Das Lakshana Parva: Digambara Jain Observance and Philosophical Content
key_dimensions: Ten virtues (Uttam Kshama, Mardav, Arjava, Shaucha, Satya, Sanyam, Tap, Tyag, Akinchanya, Brahmacharya) — direct ethical content
Based on the Tattvartha Sutra — primary Jain philosophical text accepted by both sects
Overlaps in timing with Paryushana but distinct in duration and sect — major confusion point in UPSC
Connection to Jain concept of Moksha through austerity — comparative angle with Buddhist Vassa

concepts.name: Mahavir Jayanti: Birth Anniversary and State Recognition
key_dimensions: Celebrates birth of Vardhamana Mahavira (599 BCE per Shvetambara, 615 BCE per Digambara) — sectarian dating controversy
National holiday in India — only Jain festival with this status, unlike Buddhist festivals (Buddha Purnima is also a national holiday)
Mahavira as 24th Tirthankara — distinction from the concept of a 'founder' (Jainism predates Mahavira per tradition)
Trap: Rishabhadeva/Adinatha as first Tirthankara vs. Mahavira as last — UPSC frequently tests Tirthankara sequence

concepts.name: Diwali in Jainism: Nirvana Ladnu and Sectarian Interpretation
key_dimensions: Marks Mahavira's attainment of Moksha/Nirvana at Pavapuri — same calendar date as Hindu Diwali but entirely different theological meaning
Also marks the beginning of the Jain New Year (Vira Nirvana Samvat) — distinct calendar system
New Year called 'Pratipada' — Kartik Shukla Pratipada, the day after Diwali
UPSC trap: same festival name (Diwali) shared by Hindus and Jains with fundamentally different significances — classic overlap question

concepts.name: Mauna Ekadashi and Jain Fasting Practices: Tapas and Ritual Discipline
key_dimensions: Ekadashi observed by Jains with silence (Mauna) and fasting — overlap with Hindu Ekadashi creates exam confusion
Jain fasting typology: Upvas (complete fast), Ekasana (one meal), Ayambil (tasteless food), Nivi — graded austerity system
Santhara/Sallekhana — the controversial terminal fasting practice, 2015 Rajasthan HC vs. Supreme Court debate
Constitutional angle: Sallekhana debate touches Article 21 (Right to Life) vs. religious freedom under Article 25

concepts.name: Santhara (Sallekhana): Religious Practice and Constitutional Controversy
key_dimensions: Voluntary fasting unto death — practiced by Jain monks and laity as the ultimate renunciation
2015: Rajasthan HC ruled it unconstitutional (Article 21 violation); Supreme Court stayed the order
Distinction from suicide — Jain argument: it is a conscious, non-violent, gradual process, not an act of desperation
UPSC angle: intersection of Art. 25 (freedom of religion), Art. 21 (right to life), and personal law — a rare tri-dimensional question

concepts.name: Pavarana Ceremony (Buddhist): End of Vassa and Community Reconciliation
key_dimensions: Monks invite criticism from fellow monastics at the end of Vassa — unique democratic self-correction mechanism in Sangha
Immediately precedes the Kathina robe-offering ceremony — sequential ritual logic
Reflects the Vinaya Pitaka's emphasis on monastic discipline and communal harmony
Comparative angle: similar to Jain Samvatsari (seeking forgiveness) — both are monsoon-end reconciliation rituals, a high-yield comparison

concepts.name: Bon Festival and Ancestral Veneration in Buddhist Traditions
key_dimensions: Obon (Japan) / similar ancestral veneration in Buddhist cultures — not directly Indian but relevant for comparative religion questions
In Indian context: Pitru Paksha has functional parallels — UPSC tests cross-religious concept overlap
Mahayana concept of Ullambana Sutra as textual basis — distinct from Theravada approach to ancestor veneration
Trap: Ancestor veneration in Buddhism vs. Hindu Shraddha — similar practice, different theological justification

concepts.name: Jain Pilgrimage Festivals: Mahamastakabhisheka and Shravanabelagola
key_dimensions: Mahamastakabhisheka — consecration ceremony of Gommateshvara (Bahubali) statue at Shravanabelagola, held every 12 years
Largest Jain religious gathering — Digambara tradition specifically, not Shvetambara
UNESCO consideration for intangible cultural heritage — India's nomination angle
Distinction between Bahubali (son of Rishabhadeva) and a Tirthankara — Bahubali is venerated but not a Tirthankara, a classic UPSC trap

concepts.name: Navapad Oli (Ayambil Oli): Shvetambara Jain Festival of Nine Virtues
key_dimensions: Nine-day fasting festival observed twice a year (Ashwin and Chaitra months) — biannual nature is distinctive
Worships the Navapad (nine supreme beings): Arihanta, Siddha, Acharya, Upadhyaya, Sadhu, and four others
Ayambil fasting — eating only one tasteless meal — tests knowledge of Jain fasting gradations
Less known than Paryushana but equally significant doctrinally — UPSC may test as an obscure but important festival

concepts.name: Ambedkarite Buddhist Festivals: Conversion Day and Socio-Political Dimension
key_dimensions: October 14, 1956 — Ambedkar's mass conversion at Nagpur (Dhamma Deeksha) — now celebrated as 'Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din'
Navayana Buddhism — Ambedkar's reinterpretation: rejected caste, karma-as-fatalism, and rituals — distinct from traditional Buddhism
Annual pilgrimage to Deeksha Bhoomi, Nagpur — one of the largest peaceful gatherings in the world
Constitutional angle: conversion movement intersects with Art. 25 (freedom of conscience), anti-conversion laws, and Scheduled Caste status loss upon conversion — high UPSC sensitivity

concepts.name: Kathina Ceremony: Lay-Monastic Relationship in Theravada Buddhism
key_dimensions: Held in the month after Vassa — laity offer specially woven robes (Kathina cloth) to monks
Merits for laity, discipline for monks — reciprocal religious economy of Theravada Buddhism
State patronage historically — Ashoka, Southeast Asian kings performed Kathina — linking ritual to political legitimacy
Contemporary relevance: Thailand, Sri Lanka, Myanmar diplomatic events involve Kathina — India's Buddhist diplomacy angle

concepts.name: Buddhist and Jain Festival Calendars: Lunisolar Systems and Sectarian Variations
key_dimensions: Both traditions use lunisolar calendars — Purnima (full moon) and Amavasya (new moon) as key ritual markers
Theravada uses Pali calendar; Tibetan Buddhism uses a distinct lunar calendar — causes different dates for 'same' festivals globally
Shvetambara vs. Digambara: same festival (Paryushana/Das Lakshana) on different days due to textual calendar differences
UPSC trap: questions asking which festival falls on Purnima — multiple Buddhist festivals (Buddha Purnima, Asalha, Pavarana) fall on different Purnimas, requiring precise recall
